Felix Mendelssohn. The German composer and conductor of the early Romantic period, born into a wealthy intellectual Jewish family as the grandson of philosopher Moses Mendelssohn.

He was a child prodigy who displayed mastery of Classical structure and Romantic expression at an early age. He was a key figure in musical history when in 1829 he conducted a landmark performance of J.S. Bach's St Matthew Passion, an event that sparked a major European Bach revival.

He is celebrated for his travel-inspired orchestral works. The Italian Symphony, Symphony No. 4 in A major, reflects the sunshine and folk dances of Italy and concludes with a rapid, minor-key saltarello and tarantella. The Scottish Symphony, Symphony No. 3 in A minor, was inspired by a visit to the ruins of Holyrood Chapel in Edinburgh, where Mary Queen of Scots was crowned.

His Hebrides Overture, also called Fingal's Cave, is a concert overture depicting the rolling waves and echoing acoustics of Fingal's Cave on the Scottish island of Staffa.

His most famous theatrical work is A Midsummer Night's Dream. He composed the brilliant concert overture at age seventeen and later added incidental music, which contains the ubiquitous Wedding March used at marriages.

His Violin Concerto in E minor is a cornerstone of the violin repertoire. It is noted for having the soloist enter in the very first measure and for utilizing a bassoon note to connect the first and second movements without pause.

Mendelssohn also wrote a collection of forty-eight short, lyrical piano pieces called Songs Without Words, published in eight volumes. These pieces popularized the Romantic character piece.

He was a leading conservative Romantic who maintained Classical balance. He was closely associated with the Berlin Academy of Arts alongside scientists and intellectuals of the Prussian court and conducted sacred choral works during his grand tour of Europe, visiting Rome.
